gallery.title: Size & growth
gallery.blurb:
How much research is there, and what kind? 41,657 full economic evaluations
             published 2010–2026 are included. These panels carry the headline:
             the growth of the evidence base, and how its evaluation-method mix has shifted.

figs.title: Health economic evidence is growing, and fast
figs.caption:
Annual output is growing faster than linearly — half of the literature has
                      appeared since 2020, in the last seven years of the 2010–2026 period. 41,657 eligible evaluations by publication year; 2026 is partial, against a
                      reference of cumulative growth at the 2010–2012 rate.

figs.title: Researchers increasingly exploit health's common currency: QALYs and DALYs
figs.caption:
Cost-utility analyses rose from 43% to 50% of full economic evaluations
                      (2010–2025; 2026 partial omitted) while cost-effectiveness fell from 32% to 25%.
                      Cost-utility = outcomes as DALYs or QALYs; cost-effectiveness = natural
                      outcomes (e.g. cost per death averted).

gallery.title: Topics & diseases
gallery.blurb:
What the evidence is about: the 14 harmonised disease groups (MeSH 2026 vocabulary),
             the epidemiological transition of LMIC research, and the emergent theme space — with
             the journal-finish disease figures sitting beside their companions. The topic-model
             figure ranks the emergent themes by income — from abstract embeddings (UMAP +
             HDBSCAN), not MeSH. The section also shows what the studies evaluate: the research
             space and the intervention mix by income group. Base declared on each figure.

figs.title: Which disease groups are the focus of health economic evaluations?
figs.caption:
The 14 harmonised disease groups (plus the cross-cutting C23 complications
                      tree) by share of the disease-coded literature, coloured by LMIC/HIC lean.
                      Complications & symptoms, infectious diseases and neoplasms lead; research
                      skews infectious in LMIC contexts and toward injuries and most NCD groups in
                      high-income contexts. Base: 22,744 disease-coded eligible evaluations (MeSH
                      2026 any-topic, incl. the C12.050.703 pregnancy-complications branch and F03).

figs.title: Economic evidence in LMICs shifted toward NCDs, mirroring disease burdens
figs.caption:
Disease mix of LMIC economic-evaluation research across the three transition
                      classes, against burden at both ends. In 2010, 68% of research was
                      communicable-focused vs just 42% of burden; by 2025 research much more closely
                      tracked burden. Burden: GBD 2023-round DALYs for 2010 and 2023 (IHME, mapped
                      Level-2 causes, summed over LMIC countries).

figs.title: Low- and middle-income research is tracking the epidemiological transition
figs.caption:
Journal version. Disease composition of economic-evaluation research by era (2010–17,
                      2018–26) and income group. Infectious disease is falling as a share of LMIC
                      evaluations while cancer and respiratory disease rise; high-income composition
                      is comparatively flat. Any-topic MeSH C-tree headings; bars are 95% Wilson
                      intervals, point area is the study count; both panels labelled.

figs.title: The disease areas studied are sorted by national income
figs.caption:
Journal version. Percentage of each income group's disease-coded full economic evaluations
                      that name each disease area, across the 14 harmonised groups (maternal &
                      neonatal includes the MeSH pregnancy-complications branch C12.050.703;
                      mental & substance use is MeSH F03, newly separated from neurological). Rows
                      run from areas most concentrated in low-income research (top) to high-income
                      research (bottom): infectious disease dominates lower-income groups, neoplasms
                      and cardiovascular disease the high-income group. A study naming several areas
                      appears in each, so columns sum above 100%; cells read 0 where no study named
                      the area.

figs.title: The research space by intervention type and setting
figs.caption:
A two-dimensional map of all the studies, built from abstract text embeddings
                      (UMAP-reduced and clustered; v2 run 2026-10-07, 73 clusters). Panel A colours each
                      point by its extracted primary intervention class, labelled with each class's LMIC
                      share; panel B colours the same map by LMIC share. Vaccines (41% LMIC) and
                      financing/payment policy (32%) are the most LMIC-skewed classes; devices (17%)
                      and care models (23%, with surgery close behind at 23%) are the most
                      high-income-concentrated; pharmaceuticals (30%) sit just above the 27% overall
                      share. Base: 27,930 eligible single-country studies with a known income. Classes
                      from a single-pass extraction (deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash, prompt sha 5b847afc),
                      primary class only.

figs.title: The LMIC and high-income ends of the theme space never overlap
figs.caption:
The 15 most-LMIC and 15 most-high-income of 73 emergent themes (all themes: 27%
                      LMIC). The high-income panel is shown first, plotted as each theme's
                      high-income share (a cancer theme leads at 94%); the LMIC panel as its LMIC share
                      (malaria leads at 86%). The two ends never overlap: 34–86% LMIC vs 6–15%
                       LMIC (= 85–94% high-income). n per theme = single-country studies with a
                       known income group.

figs.title: What gets evaluated — intervention mix by income
figs.caption:
Share of each income group's eligible single-country studies whose primary
                      intervention class is the given type (the optional secondary class is not
                      folded in). Pharmaceuticals peak in upper-middle-income settings (44.9%) and
                      fall to 17.2% at low income, where care-model and organisational evaluations
                      (18.3%) narrowly become the most common class; vaccines rise steadily with lower
                      income (4.8% → 14.5%) while surgery (13.7% → 6.5%) and devices (8.4% →
                      2.9%) fall. Base: 27,930 eligible single-country studies with a known World Bank
                      income group; derived by a single-pass language model
                      (deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash, temperature 0; 41,657 eligible
                      records, 1 parse failure), validated against a keyword lexicon, the emergent-topic
                      clusters and a second model lineage — no human validation available
                      (reviews/intervention-extraction.md).

gallery.title: Methods & metrics
gallery.blurb:
How the evidence base was built and how it measures outcomes: the study-selection
             funnel (PRISMA), the field's comparable metric — the QALY or DALY that lets
             cost-effectiveness be compared across diseases — how its use splits by income, and
             how often model-based vs measured evaluations report one. It closes with
             decision-usefulness by intervention type.

figs.title: From one million candidate records to 41,657 full economic evaluations
figs.caption: Study selection (PRISMA): 72,845 extracted → 41,657 eligible full economic evaluations, drawn at the foot of the spine as its two components — 39,951 articles reporting primary full evaluations and 1,706 reviews synthesising published evaluations. Reviews are retained by extraction design (framework v6.8 codes systematic, scoping and narrative reviews of published evaluations as literature/registry synthesis), so the split discloses composition and excludes nothing; 67% of strict-flagged reviews name no single country, so the country-level panels draw mostly on articles.

figs.title: The comparable metric differs by income
figs.caption:
Share of eligible evaluations reporting each comparable metric. The metric
                      flips with income: high-income research reports QALYs (54%) and almost no
                      DALYs (1%); low-income research does the reverse (40% DALYs, 9% QALYs) — so
                      rich and poor settings are measured in different units. Base: 41,657 eligible
                      evaluations (income shown for single-country studies); a study may report
                      neither, one, or both.

figs.title: Generic outcome measures are far more common in model-based than in measured evaluations
figs.caption:
Percentage of full economic evaluations reporting a generic outcome measure
                      (a QALY or DALY, which permits comparison across diseases), by how the evidence
                      was produced — decision-analytic model vs measured in patients, 2010–2026.
                      The grey bar behind each blue bar is the whole group entering that comparison.

figs.title: Decision-usefulness by intervention type — financing and care models lag
figs.caption:
Share of each intervention class's eligible evaluations whose abstract reports
                      each decision-analytic element, plus the model-based share. Financing and
                      payment-policy evaluations report an ICER in 12.0% (all eligible 36.1%), a
                      threshold in 5.8% (20.1%), uncertainty in 12.4% (32.5%) and a perspective in 7.8%
                      (22.1%); care-model and organisational evaluations follow at 19.3%, 10.8%, 16.7%
                      and 15.0%, and are the least often model-based (21.3%; all eligible 52.1%). Base:
                      each class's eligible studies against the all-eligible average; the four signals
                      are keyword matches on the abstract, so “not reported” is not “not done”.

gallery.title: Geography & authorship
gallery.blurb:
Where the research is about, and who leads it. Income-comparative figures use
             extracted geography only (the affiliation proxy is income-biased in availability);
             authorship figures use harvested affiliations and declare their denominator, including
             the income-group local-authorship estimate with its confidence intervals.

figs.title: Look north for economic evidence (mostly)
figs.caption:
Proportional-symbol map (Robinson): each bubble is a country, area =
                      evaluations naming it, colour = income group. Evidence predominates in the
                      global north. 54 of the 241 Natural Earth countries and territories have no
                      recorded evaluation — 50 of them microstates under 1M people; within the 155 countries in the map's country data only 2 (Mauritius and Eritrea) have none.

figs.title: Where the evidence is about
figs.caption:
Per-capita choropleth (Robinson): evaluations naming each country per 10
                      million people. Mid-grey = the 54 countries and territories named by no
                      eligible study (of 241 Natural Earth polygons, Antarctica excluded); pale grey
                      = named but outside the 155-country list the shading uses. 31,774
                      study–country pairs across 187 countries.

figs.title: Economic evaluations per 10 million population, by income group
figs.caption:
Density of published evaluations per 10 million population, by country and
                      World Bank income group (2010–2026); circle area is population, dashed lines
                      mark each group's median. Each circle is one of the 155 countries in the map's country data; 2 have no study and cannot be shown on the log axis. Counts are
                      study–country pairs (multi-country studies counted once per country named);
                      legend at the bottom, lowest and highest bubble labelled per group.

figs.title: Who studies whom: local authorship and collaboration
figs.caption:
Panel A: share of single-country studies with vs without an author based in
                      the country studied — 32.3% of studies about low-income countries have no
                      local author. Panel B: among studies with a local author, the income of the
                      remaining co-authors — where low-income countries do have a local author,
                      70% of those studies' other co-authors are all from high-income countries.
                      'Local' = ≥ 1 author affiliated in the country studied; n = 24,013
                      single-country eligible studies with ≥ 1 affiliation and a World Bank income
                      group.

figs.title: Most studies about a country include an author based there; Sub-Saharan Africa least often
figs.caption:
Share of single-country evaluations with at least one author based in the
                      country studied, by UN sub-region (top) and World Bank income group (bottom).
                      Most studies include a local author; Sub-Saharan Africa is lowest at 76.6%,
                      Eastern Asia highest at 98.3% (all studies: 94.5%, dashed). 'Local' = ≥ 1
                      author affiliation in the country studied; bars are 95% Wilson intervals.

figs.title: Nearly a third of studies about low-income countries have no author based there
figs.caption:
Share of single-country full economic evaluations with at least one author
                      based in the country studied, by income group (point + 95% CI). Nearly a third
                      of studies about low-income countries have no local author, against almost all
                      high-income studies. Author affiliations from the metadata harvest (available
                      for 85% of studies), 2010–2026.

figs.title: High-income teams are the hub
figs.caption:
Chord of cross-income co-authorship among 35,094 eligible evaluations with a
                      mappable affiliation income. Every income group connects mainly through high
                      income; ribbons are studies co-authored across two groups (within-group
                      excluded). Most evidence isn't cross-income at all — 25,861 studies are
                      wholly high-income-authored, just 33 wholly low-income.

gallery.title: Gaps vs disease burden
gallery.blurb:
The map's whole point: research against the burden of disease (GBD 2023 DALYs,
             country totals and 22 Level-2 causes) — per unit of burden, against a
             burden-proportional share, and within the LMIC group; the journal finishes sit beside
             their companion figures.

figs.title: Where need is high, economic evidence is scarce
figs.caption:
Studies per 100k DALYs vs total burden, one point per country (log-log, by
                      income). The median high-income country has 22× more evaluations per DALY
                      than the median low-income country. 152 countries in the map's country data with burden data and ≥ 1 study (2 more have burden but no study); burden and income are a
                      2023 snapshot against a 2010–2026 study count.

figs.title: Economic evidence is scarcest where the disease burden is greatest
figs.caption:
Journal version. Studies per 100k DALYs against total disease burden, by country and income
                      group (2023). The median high-income country sits 22× above the median
                      low-income country. Eligible full evaluations naming each country (extracted
                      geography) ÷ GBD 2023 all-cause DALYs; point area is population.

figs.title: Research share vs burden share, by disease
figs.caption:
Each disease group's share of research ÷ its share of mapped GBD burden, for
                      LMIC and HIC settings (14 harmonised groups). Maternal & neonatal research in LMIC
                      settings sits below the match line at 0.7× its burden share (a gap), against
                      5.0× in high-income settings; the largest LMIC shortfalls are injuries
                      (0.24×) and mental & substance use (0.35×). Maternal & neonatal = MeSH C16
                      plus the pregnancy-complications branch C12.050.703. LMIC n = 3,545,
                      HIC n = 11,987.

figs.title: Injuries and, in poorer settings, mental & substance use show the largest research-to-burden gaps
figs.caption:
Journal version. Research share ÷ disease-burden share for 13 of the 14 harmonised disease
                      areas (Other NCD, a residual group on both sides, is left out), by income group (points left of 1 have a smaller share of research than
                      of burden). Injuries and, in poorer settings, mental & substance use show the
                      largest gaps; maternal & neonatal is also a gap in low- and middle-income settings
                      (about 0.7×) while high-income research runs about 5× its burden share.
                      Any-topic MeSH headings; GBD 2023 DALYs for the mapped causes.

figs.title: (Un)equal weight: how research output compares with disease burden — largest gaps
figs.caption:
Diverging bars of observed − expected studies (expected = a
                      burden-proportional share of 31,627 study–country pairs). Under-served
                      countries trail negative (left), over-served positive (right): India has ~4,900
                      fewer evaluations than a proportional burden share. Bars are the 16 largest
                      deficits and 8 largest surpluses by |observed − expected| — a gap ranking,
                      not a population or burden ranking. GBD 2023 all-cause DALYs.

figs.title: (Un)equal weight: how does research output compare with disease burden? — global
figs.caption:
The burden × evidence plane (log-log) with a burden-proportional diagonal;
                      point area is population. LMICs consistently sit below the line — fewer
                      evaluations than their disease burden would suggest. 152 countries with burden
                      data and ≥ 1 study (2 more have burden but no study); GBD 2023 all-cause
                      DALYs.

figs.title: Inequity: small disease burden, few economic evaluations
figs.caption:
Lorenz curve of LMIC evidence vs LMIC disease burden (106 countries with GBD
                      data; 2 with no evaluation). Five countries hold 58% of the evidence but only
                      43% of the LMIC burden; the 41 least-served countries carrying half the burden
                      hold just 1,455 evaluations (~17%). Ordered by burden size instead, the five
                      largest-burden LMICs carry half the burden and hold 48%. Gini = 0.49.

gallery.title: Open access & funding
gallery.blurb:
How the evidence is packaged and reached. Open-access status covers 87% of the
             eligible studies (post DOI-supplement harvest); the funder field covers ~27% and is a
             floor, not a census.

figs.title: Free to read: evidence is increasingly open access
figs.caption:
Share of eligible evaluations open access, by year and income of the country
                      studied (2010–25; 2026 partial omitted). Fewer than half were open in 2010;
                      by 2025 about four in five were. The all-studies line now uses the same base as
                      the two income lines (single-country, income-known): 22,970 evaluations with an
                      OA status, of 36,360 harvested (~87% of eligible). Open-access status:
                      OpenAlex.

figs.title: Top dollar: who funds economic evaluations, and where?
figs.caption:
Top funders by eligible evaluations naming them, split by the income of the
                      country studied — the top three focused knowledge creation in high-income
                      countries. Funders are named in only ~27% of eligible studies (as-harvested,
                      lightly merged), so this is a floor and rough guide, not a census; studies
                      shown are single-country with a known income.

gallery.title: Maps & regional charts
gallery.blurb:
Three world maps (research intensity vs burden, open access, and how recent each
             country's evidence is) plus two regional bar charts (local authorship and model-based
             share, by UN sub-region). Eligible-only counts; share maps and bars show only groups
             with enough studies (grey/omitted below).

figs.title: (Un)equal weight: how does research output compare with disease burden? — global map
figs.caption:
Studies per 100k DALYs, diverging around the global median (0.67). Blue =
                      more research per unit of burden than the typical country; red = less; grey =
                      no eligible study or no GBD row. 183 of the 204 GBD countries/territories have
                      burden data and ≥ 1 study; 21 carry burden but have no study. Of the 241
                      Natural Earth polygons (Antarctica excluded), 54 are named by no study.
                      Robinson projection.

figs.title: Does evidence openness differ by geography?
figs.caption:
Share of a country's eligible evaluations that are open access, diverging
                      around the global average (71%). Blue = more open; red = more paywalled; grey =
                      fewer than 5 studies with a known status. Studies focused on North American
                      countries are more often behind paywalls; African, Eastern European and
                      Southeast Asian studies tend to be freely accessible. 133 countries with ≥ 5
                      such studies are shaded (OpenAlex OA status). Robinson projection.

figs.title: Economic evidence is growing fastest in Africa and Asia
figs.caption:
Share of a country's eligible evaluations published in 2018–2026, diverging
                      around the global average (66% of study–country pairs). Green = a newer,
                      faster-growing evidence base; grey-brown = older; blank grey = fewer than 5
                      studies. Most countries (86.2% of the 138 with ≥ 5 evaluations) had more
                      evaluations in 2018–2026 than 2010–2017, and growth was fastest in Africa
                      and Asia. Robinson projection.

figs.title: Who studies whom?
figs.caption:
Regional bar chart (reworked from the country choropleth at reviewer
                      request): share of each UN sub-region's single-country evaluations with ≥ 1
                      author based in the country studied. Sub-Saharan Africa is lowest at 76.6%,
                      Eastern Asia highest at 98.3%; every sub-region with enough studies still has a
                      local-author majority. Denominator: 23,696 single-country eligible evaluations
                      with ≥ 1 affiliation and a known sub-region (sub-regions with <50 omitted).

figs.title: Model-based vs measured evidence
figs.caption:
Regional bar chart (reworked from the country choropleth at reviewer
                      request): share of each UN sub-region's eligible evaluations built on a
                      decision model rather than measured in a study, against the global average
                      (63.9%, dashed). Latin America and the Caribbean leans on models most (78.8%),
                      Southern Asia least (57.4%). Denominator: 30,633 study–country pairs with a
                      model-based flag (sub-regions with <100 pairs omitted).

gallery.title: Trends over time
gallery.blurb:
Comparative time-series on the year dimension (2010–2025; 2026 partial, dropped).
             Income-comparative panels use single-country extracted geography with a known income
             group.

figs.title: LMICs are grabbing a growing share of the research market
figs.caption:
Share of each year's single-country evaluations about LMICs: 16% in 2010 →
                      35% in 2025 — real progress, but still far below the 83% of global disease
                      burden those countries carry (dashed line). Eligible full evaluations naming a
                      single country with a known income; 2026 partial omitted.

figs.title: Improving coverage: nearly all countries have at least one full economic evaluation
figs.caption:
Cumulative share of each income group's countries with ≥ 1 eligible
                      evaluation. Solid lines: the 155 countries in the map's country data (by 2025:
                      high income 100%, upper middle 98%, lower middle 100%, low 96%); dashed: all
                      197 World-Bank-classified countries, no population floor. Coverage looks
                      near-complete on the 155-country list, but 2 of those 155 (Eritrea, Mauritius)
                      — and 20 of 197 counting every classified country, nearly all microstates —
                      were never reached. 2026 partial omitted.

figs.title: Researchers increasingly exploit health's common currency: QALYs and DALYs
figs.caption:
Cost-utility analyses rose from 43% to 50% of full economic evaluations
                      (2010–2025; 2026 partial omitted) while cost-effectiveness fell from 32% to 25%.
                      Cost-utility = outcomes as DALYs or QALYs; cost-effectiveness = natural
                      outcomes (e.g. cost per death averted).

figs.title: CUA and CEA abstracts increasingly foreground the decision-analytic basics
figs.caption:
Share of cost-utility and cost-effectiveness evaluations whose abstract
                      foregrounds each decision-analytic element, by year (2026 partial omitted).
                      Restricted to the 28,900 CUA/CEA evaluations (of 39,056 eligible 2010–2025) —
                      only these two types report thresholds and incremental ratios. All four signals
                      rose; the cost-effectiveness threshold most, 15% → 35%. Keyword matches on the
                      abstract (records screened).

gallery.title: Priority-setting for funders
gallery.blurb:
Built for a funder asking where the next pound buys the most missing evidence.
             Ranked by gap, never by cost-to-close: there is no cost or research-funding-amount
             data. Proportionality to burden is a reference point, not a target.

figs.title: The opportunity matrix: where evidence is thinnest relative to need
figs.caption:
Disease × income research-to-burden ratio (14 harmonised groups). Deep-red
                      cells — injuries, mental & substance use, musculoskeletal and other NCD
                      in lower-income settings — are where research is most absent relative to
                      burden; maternal & neonatal is above the match line in upper-middle-income
                      settings but below it in low and lower-middle income. Grey cells have too few
                      studies (<15) to estimate. Categories are the 14 groups of the MeSH↔GBD
                      crosswalk; unmapped MeSH (e.g. signs/symptoms C23) is excluded from both sides.

figs.title: Funding priority scorecard
figs.caption:
Burden × research-intensity scatter (high-burden, low-evidence countries
                      shaded) plus the ranked bar of the 15 largest absolute shortfalls vs a
                      burden-proportional share. Eligible evaluations naming each country vs GBD 2023
                      all-cause DALYs; bubble area is population. The gap is a reference point, not a
                      target — tractability and cost also shape where research goes.

figs.title: Where to build local research capacity
figs.caption:
Burden × local-authorship share, one bubble per country (area =
                      evaluations; countries with ≥ 5). The shaded corner — high burden but
                      evidence produced largely from outside — is where funding people, not just
                      studies, matters most. Single-country eligible evaluations with an author
                      affiliation; GBD 2023 all-cause DALYs. Local authorship is a proxy for research
                      capacity, not its full measure.

figs.title: Which gaps are closing on their own, and which are stuck
figs.caption:
LMIC research-to-burden ratio per disease area, era-1 (2010–17) → era-2
                      (2018–26) arrows (14 harmonised groups). Arrows moving right toward 'matched'
                      are closing on their own; those still far left and stuck or regressing —
                      injuries, mental & substance use, other NCD and maternal & neonatal — are
                      where funding is most
                      additional. 'Closing' = era-2 ratio ≥ 5% above era-1; burden is a fixed 2023
                      LMIC reference.

figs.title: Top dollar: who funds economic evaluations, and where?
figs.caption:
Top funders by eligible evaluations naming them, split by the income of the
                      country studied — the top three focused knowledge creation in high-income
                      countries. Funders are named in only ~27% of eligible studies (as-harvested,
                      lightly merged), so this is a floor and rough guide, not a census; studies
                      shown are single-country with a known income.

hero.text:
This app maps the global evidence base of health economic evaluations — studies that
             compare two or more ways of delivering care on both costs and consequences.
full economic evaluations published 2010–2026 are included. The
presents the full figure catalogue by theme, the
lets you filter and compare studies by any variable, the
explains how the map is built.
